title: Remote collaboration with usable shared social and spatial cues

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a remote collaboration environment in which people can reliably understand who is attending to whom or what, coordinate speech and gestures, and work together on shared material. It would make cues such as gaze direction, addressee, spatial relationships and references to shared objects useful for coordinating a group. The goal is successful communication and joint work across distance; a visually convincing representation alone does not establish that outcome.

As a proposed design requirement, these cues should remain understandable without excessive setup, uncomfortable equipment or misleading representations of another person's attention. Perfect physical indistinguishability from being together is neither required by this concept nor established by the supplied evidence. Different tasks may need different combinations of attention cues, shared views, spatial audio, gestures and interaction with shared material.

significance.text: If demonstrated broadly, reliable social and spatial coordination could substantially expand the kinds of group activity that work well across distance. The direct advance would be an interaction experience in which people more readily identify an addressee, follow shared attention, find opportunities to speak and coordinate contributions. LookAtChat supplies a limited empirical basis for the attention component: its authors report improved perceived attention with gaze visualizations. That finding supports the mechanism's plausibility, but does not demonstrate the complete proposed capability.

Conditional impact synthesis: stronger remote coordination could make distributed teamwork, teaching, clinical collaboration and social contact more useful or accessible, and could reduce some travel. These outcomes would depend on adoption, task suitability, affordability, accessibility and independent evaluation in each setting. Better coordination in a conversation does not by itself establish better learning, healthcare outcomes or relationships.

Impact boundary: the useful analogy is to selected coordination advantages of sharing a room, rather than to complete replacement of physical presence. A successful system could preserve shared attention and effective collaboration while using representations that look different from ordinary face-to-face interaction. Its significance should therefore be judged through communication and task outcomes, alongside participants' experience and practical burdens, rather than through visual realism alone.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central capability still requiring convincing demonstration in the supplied record is reliable integration of social cues and shared work across varied group activities. The LookAtChat paper documents difficulties with identifying addressees, timing speech, conveying gestures and working with shared material, as well as constraints involving equipment cost, availability, calibration and privacy. Its gaze-awareness prototype addresses part of this problem; the supplied evidence does not establish that these components have been combined into a broadly effective collaboration environment.

Engineering synthesis: a system must capture or infer relevant attention and gestures, map them into a shared spatial frame and display them in a way that participants interpret correctly. It must distinguish attention directed at another participant from attention directed at shared material, and make those relationships understandable as layouts and viewpoints change. Inaccurate or ambiguous cues could make coordination harder by suggesting an addressee or focus that the participant did not intend.

Engineering synthesis: speech, gesture and changes to shared material must also remain sufficiently synchronized under delay, packet loss and heterogeneous devices. More participants create more possible attention relationships and more opportunities for visual clutter. The scientific challenge is to determine which representations improve actual coordination, for which tasks and populations, and whether benefits persist with repeated use. Accessibility, fatigue, privacy, setup effort and cost are proposed practical constraints on that capability, rather than experimentally established necessities with identical thresholds for every task.

current_state.text: Video conferencing and spatial collaboration systems already support remote communication and work. The specific research evidence supplied here concerns Zhenyi He, Ruofei Du and Ken Perlin's LookAtChat preprint, arXiv:2107.06265, DOI 10.48550/arXiv.2107.06265, submitted on 13 July 2021 and revised on 5 August 2021. The landing page calls it “LookAtChat: Visualizing Gaze Awareness for Remote Small-Group Conversations,” while the supplied version 3 PDF uses “LookAtChat: Visualizing Eye Contacts for Remote Small-Group Conversations.” The supplied review identifies both as the same work through the authors, identifier and version date.

LookAtChat explored webcam-based gaze visualization in an exploratory study of 20 participants arranged into four five-person groups. The groups compared a baseline layout, a 2D directional layout and a 3D perspective layout during short conversations and a party game. This provides evidence about small-group gaze awareness under those study conditions, rather than a demonstration of the full range of collaborative work envisioned by this concept.

The authors report improved perceived attention and selected social-experience ratings, but no significant effects on other conversation-experience questions. These findings should not be extended into claims of reliably improved turn-taking, joint manipulation, equivalence to physical co-location or long-term effectiveness. Conversely, the absence of significant effects on those questions in a small exploratory study does not establish that broader benefits are impossible. The review also identifies limitations involving the participant population, shared presentations and network conditions.

The supplied review assessed PDF text spanning all 23 pages, including methods, results and limitations, so the earlier abstract-only characterization is inaccurate for the evidence now available. The source index records an untruncated extraction with a numeric parsing warning; figure images were not inspected in the supplied review. Those limitations do not obstruct the textual findings summarized here, but they constrain interpretation of figure-dependent details. This record relies on that supplied review and does not imply a new inspection of the paper.

Evidence boundary: the supplied freshness-search record is empty. Consequently, the state of the wider field as of 1 November 2026 remains unverified. The dated 2021 preprint remains evidence for its reported prototype and study, but cannot establish present-day availability, later progress or whether the broader capability remains unsolved across all existing systems.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: independent evaluators should compare remote groups using the system with co-located groups and strong existing video or spatial collaboration systems. Evaluations should include unscripted conversations and collaborative tasks requiring shared attention, speech coordination, gestures and joint work on shared material. Before testing, investigators should specify task-appropriate success thresholds, acceptable trade-offs, and the populations and settings to which a successful result would apply. These are proposed criteria, not an established standard.
completion_criteria.label: Independent group comparisons use prespecified task success thresholds

completion_criteria.text: Proposed measures should combine perceived attention and social experience with observed turn-taking, successful references to people and objects, coordination errors and task outcomes. This separation matters because the supplied LookAtChat study reported attention benefits without significant effects on other conversation-experience questions. A convincing evaluation should establish which outcomes improve, rather than treating a favorable attention rating as evidence that every aspect of collaboration has improved.
completion_criteria.label: Attention measures and observed collaboration outcomes distinguish demonstrated benefits

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical evaluation should include more than two participants, varied group sizes, repeated use, imperfect networks and heterogeneous devices. It should assess accessibility, fatigue, privacy, setup and calibration effort, cost and participants' preferences, including whether people continue to choose the system after initial novelty. Results should make clear when particular equipment, network conditions or participant capabilities are necessary.
completion_criteria.label: Repeated group evaluations assess practical burdens and necessary conditions

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility requirement: independent teams should be able to reproduce the central benefits using documented system configurations, tasks and analysis methods. Convincing completion would mean a clearly bounded capability with replicated advantages and disclosed limitations. Finite evaluations establish demonstrated breadth across the tested conditions; they cannot establish literal universality or suitability for every form of remote collaboration.
completion_criteria.label: Independent teams reproduce central benefits with disclosed limitations

related_concepts.text: Roster-based comparison: HCI-07, “Everyday visual computing with perceptually convincing spatial displays,” concerns the visual presentation that could help people perceive shared space. HCI-03, “A general-purpose, high-fidelity interface for touch and physical force,” concerns physical feedback that could support some joint activities. Both may contribute to HCI-11, but display quality or realistic touch alone does not demonstrate successful multi-person communication and coordination. Neither capability is a blanket prerequisite for every useful implementation of this concept.

Roster-based comparison: HCI-08, “Real-time conversational interfaces across signed and spoken languages,” overlaps communication across participants, while HCI-04, “An interface that makes inaccessible software operable through a user’s chosen modality,” overlaps access to collaboration tools. Their distinct goals concern language mediation and software operability. HCI-11 concerns shared attention and group coordination, which must also be evaluated when participants use different languages or modalities.

Roster-based comparison: HCI-09, “Privacy controls that remain understandable and enforceable across services,” is relevant when collaboration systems capture attention, gestures or shared work. HCI-11 must account for the privacy consequences of those features, while HCI-09 addresses the broader problem of understandable and enforceable controls across services. HCI-01, “A predictive science of human–computer interaction,” could inform explanations and predictions of coordination outcomes; HCI-11 remains a particular interaction capability whose effectiveness requires empirical demonstration.

Scope of these comparisons: they are conceptual distinctions based on the supplied roster titles and the candidate's descriptions, especially its stated overlaps with HCI-07 and HCI-03. Full records for those other innovations were not supplied. These relationships do not establish their technical dependencies, merge their identities or imply that progress on one completes another.

unresolved_issues: No freshness-search evidence was supplied, so subsequent progress and present-day availability as of 1 November 2026 remain unverified.
The supplied review did not inspect figure images, and the PDF extraction records a numeric parsing warning. Figure-dependent details are therefore not resolved here.

The supplied review does not provide numerical effect sizes, confidence intervals or exact significance values for the reported benefits; their magnitude and precision remain unspecified in this record.
Task-specific success thresholds, acceptable trade-offs and intended populations remain to be defined for any actual completion demonstration.
Whether attention benefits generalize to sustained turn-taking improvements, joint manipulation, diverse populations and repeated real-world use is not established by the supplied study.
Full records for the related concepts were not supplied, so detailed technical dependencies and overlaps beyond the roster-based comparisons remain unresolved.

brief.title: Remote teamwork with clear attention and gestures
possible: People working apart could reliably tell who someone is addressing, what they are looking at and how a gesture relates to shared material. Groups could use those signals to find moments to speak and coordinate work across distance.
why: This could expand the kinds of teamwork, teaching, clinical collaboration and social contact that work well remotely. Clearer coordination could make participation more accessible and reduce some travel.

sources.who: Zhenyi He, Ruofei Du and Ken Perlin
sources.showed: Their preprint, a paper shared before peer review, describes LookAtChat. It uses ordinary webcams to show who is looking at whom. A small exploratory study found improved perceived attention and some social-experience ratings.
sources.quote: LookAtChat tracks each user’s gaze direction, identifies who is looking at whom, and provides corresponding spatial cues.
sources.cited_for: Showing where people look can help participants feel that others are paying attention.
sources.not_established: The study did not establish reliable improvements in taking turns, working on shared objects or sustained collaboration.

sources.who: Huidong Bai, Prasanth Sasikumar, Jing Yang and Mark Billinghurst
sources.showed: They combined a live view of a worker’s surroundings with an expert’s looking direction and hand gestures. Together, these signals made spatial instructions easier to convey than looking direction alone.
sources.quote:
The combined cues were 
also rated signiﬁcantly higher than the gaze in terms of ease 
of conveying spatial actions.
sources.cited_for: Combining looking direction and gestures can improve remote guidance and the feeling of being together.
sources.not_established: An expert guiding a worker does not establish reliable coordination across varied group activities.

sources.who: Kate Nowak, Lev Tankelevitch, John Tang and Sean Rintel
sources.showed: They tested spatial audio, which makes voices sound as though they come from different locations, with 75 employees. Participants reported greater interactivity, shared space and ease of understanding.
sources.quote:
Spatial audio increased perceptions of interactivity, shared
space, and ease of understanding.
sources.cited_for: Separating voices by apparent location can improve how a remote conversation feels.
sources.not_established: Task performance did not improve significantly, and preferences were divided.

shown: Researchers have demonstrated useful pieces of the capability. He and colleagues tested webcam-based attention signals in an exploratory study with 20 participants. Bai and colleagues combined looking direction and gestures for remote guidance; Nowak and colleagues tested voices placed at different apparent locations.
missing: A combined system still needs to demonstrate reliable attention, speech, gestures and shared work across varied group activities.
Benefits need to persist across repeated use, different devices, larger groups and imperfect networks.
Independent teams need to reproduce the central benefits while measuring accessibility, fatigue, privacy, setup effort and cost.

milestones.label: Independent comparisons meet success thresholds set before testing
milestones.explanation: Independent comparisons with groups sharing a room and strong existing remote tools would have to meet task-specific thresholds set before testing. This would establish where the system supports successful group work.

milestones.label: Attention ratings and observed teamwork reveal distinct benefits
milestones.explanation: Evaluations would have to measure perceived attention alongside observed speaking turns, references, errors and task results. This would distinguish feeling attended to from working together more effectively.

milestones.label: Repeated group use reveals burdens and necessary conditions
milestones.explanation: Repeated group studies would have to assess varied group sizes, devices, networks, preferences and practical burdens. This would establish when people can and choose to keep using the system.

milestones.label: Independent teams reproduce benefits and disclose limits
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to reproduce the central benefits using documented systems, tasks and methods. This would establish a dependable capability with clear limits across the conditions tested.

uncertain: It remains unclear which combinations of signals help which tasks and populations.
Better perceived attention may not lead to lasting improvements in speaking turns or shared work.
Task-specific success thresholds and acceptable trade-offs still need to be defined.

page.title: Collaborative telepresence
page.definition: A remote collaboration system conveys whom people address, where they direct their attention, and how speech and gestures refer to shared objects. Groups use these social and spatial cues to coordinate conversation and joint work.

goal.need: In 2020, a 24-person experiment found faster shared manipulation with combined gaze and gesture cues. In 2023, a 75-person experiment found improved perceived interactivity with spatial audio, but no significant pooled survival-task benefit. These results motivate testing integrated systems against joint-task outcomes as well as perceived interaction.

figures.caption: Completion times for a remote brick pick-and-place task.
figures.note: Twelve participant pairs; Control omitted the shared gaze and gesture cues.

statements.quote: change their view, move about in the world, manipulate the world, gesture, and generally act and communicate with more than just their voice.
statements.context: Capabilities the white paper says remote users need in enterprise and workplace communication.

statements.quote: Apply eXtended Reality technologies to support the communication and collaboration experience;
statements.context: An objective of topic HORIZON-CL4-2021-HUMAN-01-25; the cited page was updated on 27 June 2022.

completion.title: Independent teams reproduce a joint-task benefit from integrated collaborative telepresence.
completion.criterion: For a specified task, population and device/network configuration, remote groups use one system conveying addressees, gaze targets, speech turns, gestures and references to shared objects. Against the same interface without the added cues, groups complete the shared task faster or more accurately, with p < 0.05 under an analysis correcting for multiple comparisons where applicable. An independent team reproduces the benefit under the same task conditions. The claim is limited to that tested use case.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas fallback; no external end-to-end acceptance test was located.
completion.basis: Searched ITU-T F.734 and G.1091, IEEE's telepresence white paper and Horizon Europe's telepresence call for an integrated joint-work acceptance test; none specifies one. This fallback extends the studies' comparative task-performance test to an integrated system and requires independent reproduction. It establishes a bounded task benefit, not equivalence to physical co-location.

milestones.title: A video telepresence system conveys both direct and averted gaze.
milestones.criterion: Meet F.734 User02: users perceive mutual looking and looking toward another person or object, with participant images within tolerable gaze-direction angles in both axes. Its note cites research suggesting 3–5° horizontally, up to 12° upward and 8° downward; no identification-accuracy cutoff is given. LookAtChat's 2021 preprint tested 20 people in four five-person groups and improved perceived attention; this does not establish the full requirement.
milestones.set_by: ITU-T F.734 (2014), User02 and Note 1; written for video telepresence.
milestones.threshold_quote: awareness of both direct gaze and averted gaze

milestones.title: Telepresence users identify the talking participant at the correct spatial location.
milestones.criterion: Meet G.1091 section 7.5: every seat receives directional audio, and the talking participant is identified in the correct spatial geometry. Nowak et al.'s experiment analysed 15 groups and 30 meetings: perceived interactivity improved (p = .023), but the study did not establish conformity with this spatial-identification requirement.
milestones.set_by: ITU-T G.1091 (2014), section 7.5; written for room-based telepresence.
milestones.threshold_quote: The person who is talking shall be identified in correct spatial geometry.

milestones.title: Shared gaze and gestures reduce remote pick-and-place time at the .05 significance level.
milestones.criterion: In Bai et al.'s task, a remote expert guides a local worker through four brick pick-and-place subtasks. Sharing gaze and hand gestures reduces completion time relative to the Control condition at the .05 significance level, with Bonferroni adjustment. The experiment met this comparison (p = .005); its times appear in the goal table. This establishes a benefit for the specified dyadic task.
milestones.set_by: Comparative HCI user-study convention, instantiated by Bai et al., CHI 2020, Measurements and Results; the task and outcome are study-specific.
milestones.threshold_quote: The mean difference was signiﬁcant at the .05 level

milestones.title: An integrated telepresence system improves group-task performance in a real-use setting.
milestones.criterion: In a real-use setting, remote groups use one system conveying addressees, gaze targets, speech turns, gestures and references to shared objects. Relative to the same interface with the added cues disabled, joint-task completion is faster or more accurate, with p < 0.05 under an analysis correcting for multiple comparisons where applicable. This is the initial integrated result, before independent reproduction. Horizon Europe calls for end-user tests in real environments but supplies no joint-task improvement threshold.
milestones.set_by: Technology Atlas fallback: searches of ITU-T F.734/G.1091, the IEEE white paper and the Horizon Europe call found no integrated group-task performance threshold.

not_found: No agreed minimum task-performance gain or end-user sample size was located for integrated collaborative telepresence.
No independent reproduction of the full integrated group-task test stated here was located.
The ETH-hosted Bai PDF and ACM landing page could not be opened; an author-uploaded full text was accessible.

results.finding: Among 20 participants, reported eye contact was higher with the directional layout than baseline (p < .002).
results.detail: The questionnaire asked whether participants wanted to or did make eye contact. The study did not establish perception of both mutual and averted gaze within the required horizontal and vertical angles.
results.quote:
Post hoc t-tests with Bonferroni correction showed significant differences between
baseline layout and directional layout (𝑝 <.002∗∗) with a ‘large’ effect size (Cohen’s d >.8).

results.finding: In 12 pairs, combined gaze and gesture cues reduced brick-task completion time versus Control (p = .005).
results.detail: The four-subtask pick-and-place comparison used a Bonferroni-corrected post hoc analysis.
results.quote:
A
Post Hoc analysis using the Bonferroni correction revealed
that the time (in seconds) to complete the tasks with Combined
cues (M = 139.08, SD = 44.99) was statistically signiﬁcantly
faster than the Control condition (M = 227.75, SD = 88.76,
p = .005).

results.finding: In 12 pairs, combined gaze and gesture cues reduced task completion time versus Control (p = .005).
results.detail: The study used a simplified task in a controlled environment. It shared gaze and gestures in one direction and did not establish all required integrated cues or a real-use result.
results.quote:
A
Post Hoc analysis using the Bonferroni correction revealed
that the time (in seconds) to complete the tasks with Combined
cues (M = 139.08, SD = 44.99) was statistically signiﬁcantly
faster than the Control condition (M = 227.75, SD = 88.76,
p = .005).

results.finding: Among 75 participants, spatial audio improved perceived conversation interactivity (p = .023).
results.detail: Audio positions matched participants’ screen positions, but the study did not establish that users identified speakers at the correct spatial locations. Some participants reported spatial position confusion.
results.quote:
Using the non-parametric Wilcoxon signed-rank test, sur-
vey statement S5, “The conversation seemed highly interactive”,
was statistically significant at the 5% level (z=-2.281, p=0.023).

results.finding: Among 15 groups, survival-task performance was not significantly improved with spatial audio.
results.detail: The study compared spatial and mono audio in simulated survival tasks. It did not test an integrated system conveying all required cues in a real-use setting.
results.quote:
On average, groups performed better on the tasks in the spatial
audio condition. However, these results were not statistically sig-
nificant.

results.finding: ConnectBoard users reported eye contact and correctly inferred gaze toward shared media in 1-on-1 meetings; sample size not reported.
results.detail: The paper reports user observations but does not give measured gaze-direction angles in both axes or enough detail to establish the specified tolerances.
results.quote:
In
our experiments, users reported that they were able to make
eye contact with remote users, and they were also able to
correctly infer the gaze direction with respect to shared media,
as shown in Fig. 11.

results.finding: LiveMask’s reduced face-shaped screen: 5 participants identified gaze direction with 44.5% accuracy.
results.detail: Participants judged prerecorded gaze at seven horizontal positions. The study did not establish the required gaze-direction tolerances in both axes or demonstrate the full requirement in live interaction.

results.finding: In listening tests with 32 subjects, 76% correctly localized virtual talkers in the frontal placement.
results.detail: The test used prerecorded speech and headphones, with one listener and one talker at a time. It did not establish that every seat receives directional audio or that G.1091 section 7.5 is met.
results.quote:
76 percent
of the subjects correctly localized virtual talkers in Frontal
placement-1, which is the best result among all tests.

results.finding: In 40 in-room participants, augmented multichannel audio made identifying who was speaking easier than mono (p = 0.012).
results.detail: Participants watched prerecorded conversations from center or side seats. The study did not establish that every seat received directional audio or that each talking participant was identified in the correct spatial geometry.
results.quote: Pairwise comparisons showed that participants rated the Augmented Multichannel condition as easier than the Mono condition (p = 0.012; Figure 3a).

results.finding: ConnectBoard users reported eye contact and correct gaze inference in 1-on-1 meetings; the sample size was not stated.
results.detail: The prototype supports gaze awareness and shared media, but the paper reports no controlled real-use joint-task performance comparison or statistical significance.
results.quote:
In
our experiments, users reported that they were able to make
eye contact with remote users, and they were also able to
correctly infer the gaze direction with respect to shared media,
as shown in Fig. 11.

results.finding: Five participants identified gaze direction with 44.5% accuracy using a downsized face-shaped screen.
results.detail: This tests recognition of one social cue using photographs, not integrated remote group-task performance in a real-use setting.

results.finding: In MultiView’s 23-participant study, 90% of gaze judgments were at most one target off.
results.detail: Participants reported eye contact both for direct and averted gaze, with little difference between directions. The setup had about 3° average vertical parallax and no horizontal parallax, but the study does not establish tolerable angles for all participant images in both axes.
results.quote: For the condition of gaze, 90% of the responses were at most one target oﬀ.

results.finding: Gazing Heads: 20 groups of four tested a simulation; head rotation clearly conveyed gaze and enhanced perceived attention.
results.detail: The study reports direct eye contact and gaze toward other participants, but gives no gaze-direction angles or result for looking toward objects. The tested system was a camera-based simulation.
results.quote: We conducted a user study comparing Gazing Heads with a conventional „Tiled View“ video conferencing system, for 20 groups of 4 people, on each of two tasks. The study found that head rotation clearly conveys gaze and strongly enhances the perception of attention.

results.finding: In a four-speaker test, 16 subjects correctly identified the speaker 88% of the time with spatial audio.
results.detail: Subjects used headphones and prerecorded sentences. The experiment did not establish directional audio at every seat or verify correct spatial geometry under G.1091 section 7.5.
results.quote:
Experiments in
which subjects had to identify the active speaker out of
a number of possibilities, demonstrate that spatial audio
affords the user an approximately two-fold increase in
correct speaker identiﬁcation rate in a conference call.
